metaTitle: Best RV Generators for Every Rig Size (2026)
metaDescription: Six RV generators compared by rated watts, fuel type, noise and weight, from a quiet inverter for a small trailer to a 4,500 watt unit for large rigs.
expertTake: The Westinghouse 5000 Dual Fuel is our top pick for most RV owners because it delivers 3,900 rated watts, clean power, remote start and a propane option from a brand with real parts support. The PowerSmart 4300 is the value pick. If your RV already has a built-in generator that runs weekly, you may not need a portable at all.
introParagraphs: An RV generator has one job that never changes: keep the air conditioner and the battery charger running when the campground has no power. Everything else, from noise to fuel type to weight, is a trade against that single demand.

The market splits into quiet inverter machines and cheaper open-frame ones, and into gasoline-only and dual fuel designs. This guide ranks six machines that cover the common rigs and explains where each one stops being enough.

products.name: Westinghouse 5000 Peak Watt Dual Fuel Inverter, Remote Start
products.description:
The Westinghouse earns first place by doing many things competently. It delivers 3,900 rated watts, which is enough for a 13,500 BTU air conditioner plus normal loads, and it adds a propane option, remote start and a rotating display showing fuel level, output, runtime and voltage. Distortion is under 3 percent, so a laptop or CPAP is safe.

The design is an inverter with a telescoping handle and wheels, so it moves like a small suitcase. The remote key fob lets you start it from inside the coach. Propane drops the output, as it does for every dual fuel unit, so read the manual for the figure before you rely on it for an air conditioner.

Upkeep is typical for a modern inverter. Change the oil after the first 20 hours, run on propane now and then to keep the regulator supple, and keep the starter battery charged. Compared with the iGen4000DF in this family it adds 600 rated watts, which is the reason to buy this one. In practice that margin is what lets the microwave run while the compressor cycles, instead of tripping the overload light every time someone makes coffee.
products.bestFor: Most RV owners who want output, clean power and convenience from one machine.
pros: 3,900 rated watts covers one air conditioner and more
cons: Not enough for two air conditioners

products.name: PowerSmart 4300 Watt Inverter Generator, 12 Hour Runtime
products.description:
PowerSmart's pitch is long runtime at a modest cost. A 1.9 gallon tank claims up to 12 hours at a quarter load, and 3,500 running watts is enough for one air conditioner and a few appliances. The under 3 percent distortion rating suits electronics.

It is gasoline only, so it lacks the propane flexibility of the Westinghouse. That keeps cost down and complexity low, which is exactly why it is the value choice. The brand is newer, so verify the warranty.

A quarter load claim means lights and chargers, not an air conditioner, so expect fewer hours under a heavy load. Rated watts fall 400 short of the Westinghouse 5000, and so does the price. Run the carburetor dry before storage and change the oil early. Because the tank is small and the brand is newer, carry a spare plug and filter and keep the manual where you can find it.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a gasoline inverter with long light-load runtime at a low cost.
pros: 1.9 gallon tank claims 12 hours at quarter load
3,500 running watts for one air conditioner
Lower cost than the major brands

products.name: EFURDEN 4300W Inverter Generator, 30A RV Ready, USB-C
products.description:
The cleanest power in the lineup comes from this unit: under 2 percent distortion, with a USB-C QC 3.0 port and a 30 amp outlet. A trailer full of electronics benefits from that waveform.

It runs five hours at half load on the listing, shorter than the PowerSmart's claim, so it suits owners who run it for a few hours a day rather than overnight. At 3,300 running watts it covers one air conditioner with care.

The brand has a thin support network, so register the warranty. A quick oil check and a clear set of vents before each run is the whole routine. Compared with the PowerSmart 4300, it adds cleaner power and charging ports but gives less runtime. Owners who use it as a daytime charger for batteries and devices, rather than a night-long unit, get the best of it.
products.bestFor: RVs full of electronics that run the generator a few hours a day.
pros: Under 2 percent THD is very clean
30 amp outlet plus two 20 amp outlets
cons: Five hours at half load is short

products.name: WEN GN5600 5600 Watt Generator, Transfer Switch and RV Ready

specList.label: Runtime
specList.value: Up to 12.5 hours at half load

products.description:
This is the conventional workhorse: a 224cc open-frame engine making 4,500 running watts, a 4.3 gallon tank and a claimed 12.5 hours at half load. A wheel and handle kit makes it movable, and it is both transfer switch and RV ready.

It is louder than any inverter and gives dirtier power, so it suits owners who prioritize capacity and cost over quiet. The 4,500 running watts beats every inverter here except the WEN 6800, and is enough for an air conditioner plus a microwave.

It serves as home backup too, which is a bonus for a dual-use buyer. Keep the oil full, store the fuel stable and run it monthly. It adds 600 rated watts and a bigger tank over the Westinghouse 5000, but without quiet or remote start. A neighbor at the next site will hear it clearly, so use it where rules and distance allow, and keep it on a level pad so the oil sensor reads correctly.
products.bestFor: Owners who want capacity, runtime and home backup at a modest cost.
pros: 4.3 gallon tank claims 12.5 hours at half load

products.name: WEN 6800 Watt Dual Fuel RV Ready Inverter, CO Watchdog
products.description:
The WEN 6800 is where an RV owner goes when 3,900 watts is not enough. At 5,100 rated on gasoline and 4,500 on propane it can run two air conditioners with some care, and it is still an inverter, so noise is moderate.

The CO Watchdog shuts the engine off if carbon monoxide builds up, and the bonded-neutral 240 volt configuration allows low-power vehicle charging. These are practical extras for a large rig.

It is heavy, so plan a ramp or a truck. That is 1,200 more rated watts than the Westinghouse 5000. Run it monthly and keep the oil full. A machine with 5,100 rated watts working at 70 percent load for hours runs hot, so give it space on all sides and never box it in with a cover while it runs.
products.bestFor: Large rigs with two air conditioners that want inverter quiet.
pros: 5,100 rated watts handles two air conditioners
Dual fuel with 4,500 rated watts on propane
cons: Costs more than the 4,000 watt class

products.name: Westinghouse iGen4000DF 4000 Peak Watt Dual Fuel Inverter
products.description:
This version of the iGen4000DF adds remote start to the recoil model, so a trailer owner can fire it from the couch. At 3,300 rated watts it suits a single air conditioner rig with modest extras.

It shares the data center, clean power and propane option of the bigger sibling in a lighter frame. That makes it easier to lift into a bumper rack.

It costs more than the recoil version, and the 3,300 rated watts is tight with an air conditioner and microwave. Run it monthly and keep the battery charged. A trailer owner who lifts it onto a bumper rack should confirm the rack rating first, since a falling generator on a highway is a serious hazard.
products.bestFor: Small to mid trailers that want remote start and propane in a lighter frame.
cons: 3,300 rated watts is tight with a microwave
Costs more than the recoil version

buyingCriteria.explanation: A 13,500 BTU roof unit needs 2,500 to 3,000 watts to start and 1,500 to run. The Westinghouse 5000 at 3,900 rated and PowerSmart 4300 at 3,500 running cover one, while two need the WEN 6800 at 5,100 rated. Count your roof units before anything else, and check each nameplate for its running amps, since an older 15,000 BTU unit can draw noticeably more than a newer 13,500 BTU one. A soft start kit cuts the starting surge and is the cheapest way to let a smaller generator carry an air conditioner.

An inverter converts to DC and back for clean power and a throttle that follows load. The WEN GN5600 open frame gives 4,500 running watts for less money but louder. For a campground with quiet hours, choose inverter, because a fixed-speed open frame at 70 dBA or more at the pad is the machine neighbors complain about first. Power quality also matters if the RV has a modern converter, TV board or CPAP.

Propane stores for years and suits an RV that already carries it. The Westinghouse 5000 and WEN 6800 are dual fuel, losing about 10 percent of output on propane. Gasoline-only units like the PowerSmart 4300 are simpler, with fewer fittings that can leak or stiffen, and they cost less. If you rarely store the machine for long, the simplicity may outweigh the propane benefit.

The PowerSmart claims 12 hours at quarter load and the EFURDEN 5 hours at half load. A number with no load basis is meaningless. Halve any claim for real air conditioner use, and expect even less in hot weather when the compressor runs almost continuously. Carry a spare can so a mid-trip refuel does not become a drive to town.

Larger machines need a ramp or a truck. Open frames like the GN5600 are heavy. Check your storage method before buying, and measure the bay or rack, since several of these frames are wider than they look in the photos. A machine that does not fit its storage place ends up riding in the cabin, which is neither safe nor pleasant.

A CO sensor, like the WEN 6800's Watchdog, shuts the engine down if gas builds up. It does not replace outdoor placement. Low oil protection stops a run but protects the engine, and a sudden shutdown is a prompt to check the dipstick, not to restart it repeatedly. Never remove or bypass these sensors.

specDecoder.meaning: Continuous output the machine holds. This is the number to compare with the sum of the appliances you expect to run together.
Short surge for motors. It lasts a second or two, so it helps a compressor start but cannot carry a load.
Waveform cleanliness, measured as how far the output departs from a perfect sine wave. A lower percentage is gentler on sensitive circuit boards.
The load at which hours are quoted. A claim at quarter load will look far better than the same machine at full load.
specDecoder.watchFor: The GN5600 states 12.5 hours at half load.

specDecoder.meaning: An outlet that can feed a house transfer switch. It is useful when the same machine doubles as home backup during an outage.

howWeEvaluated.title: Rig fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared rated watts to common rigs. The Westinghouse 5000 suits one air conditioner, the WEN 6800 two. We assumed a 13,500 BTU roof unit as the benchmark load and added a microwave and a battery charger on top.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fuel options
howWeEvaluated.description: Dual fuel and propane output were considered. The WEN 6800 gives 4,500 on propane, a drop of about 600 watts from gasoline, and that loss was weighed against machines that publish no propane number at all.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise and power quality
howWeEvaluated.description: Inverter designs scored higher than open frame. The EFURDEN under 2 percent THD led, with the Westinghouse and PowerSmart units at under 3 percent close behind. Open-frame output without a published figure was treated as the weakest option for electronics.

howWeEvaluated.title: Runtime honesty
howWeEvaluated.description: Listings with a load basis scored higher. The GN5600 figure of 12.5 hours at half load is a useful one, and the EFURDEN five hours at half load shows how wide the spread is between tank sizes.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on owner feedback patterns, we weighed brand support and parts. Westinghouse and WEN scored well, since both publish manuals, part numbers and service contacts that make a repair possible far from home.

rows: Typical travel trailer, one air conditioner

cards.label: Inverter (Westinghouse, WEN 6800, PowerSmart)
cards.text: Quiet, clean and efficient at light load, with an engine that slows down at night when only a fridge and lights run. The Westinghouse 5000 adds remote start, and the PowerSmart 4300 adds a long quarter-load runtime.

cards.label: Open frame (WEN GN5600)
cards.text: Higher output per cost and home backup, but louder with dirtier power, and a fixed engine speed that burns the same fuel at light load as at heavy load. It is the right tool for a driveway and a storm, and a compromise at a quiet campground.

howToChoose.note: Choose inverter for campgrounds; choose open frame for capacity and cost.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Quiet inverter design, low noise at part load, and clean power. Place the machine away from neighbors, point the exhaust away from tents and windows, and set it on a rubber mat to reduce vibration carried through the ground.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Westinghouse 5000 and iGen4000DF are the best fit, with the WEN 6800 for larger rigs.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You run two air conditioners or want propane and remote start. The WEN 6800 and Westinghouse 5000 justify it, because the extra cost buys output headroom, a CO shutoff or a convenience you will use every trip.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You run light loads or camp mostly with hookups. The PowerSmart 4300 or WEN GN5600 covers it without paying for features you will not use.

maintenance.why: Small crankcases hold little oil and run hot. Low oil stops the run, and running low can score the cylinder wall.
Gasoline gums jets within weeks, especially ethanol blends. Use stabilizer or run the carburetor dry before putting the machine away.
Remote and electric start depend on it.

faq.q: What size RV generator do I need?
faq.a: One air conditioner needs about 3,500 to 3,900 rated watts. Two need around 5,000. Count your roof units and appliances, and add the starting surge of the largest compressor to the running load of everything else.

faq.q: Is an inverter generator worth it for an RV?
faq.a: For quiet and clean power, yes. Open frames cost less per watt but are louder.

faq.q: Which is the best budget choice?
faq.a: The PowerSmart 4300 is the lowest cost inverter, while the WEN GN5600 is the lowest cost per watt.

Usually, since RVs carry propane. Expect about 10 percent less output on propane, as on the WEN 6800 where 5,100 rated watts becomes 4,500, and exercise the propane side now and then so the regulator stays supple.

faq.q: Can I run it at a campground?
faq.a: Only where rules allow and during permitted hours. Quiet inverters are accepted more often.
Outdoors, on level ground, well away from windows and doors. Never run it in an enclosed space, a garage or a storage bay, and keep a battery-powered carbon monoxide detector inside the RV.
